outcome: The general problem (a combinatorial rule for all Kronecker coefficients g(lambda,mu,nu)) remains open, but Pak, Panova and Swanson (arXiv:2511.02312, first posted 4 November 2025) proved an explicit positive combinatorial interpretation, via counting certain marked trees, for the rectangular Kronecker coefficients g(lambda,(n^k),(n^k)) in the special case where lambda has at most two rows -- a genuine settled sub-case of the stated problem, not merely a related/variant problem.
summary: The stated problem -- give a combinatorial interpretation of the Kronecker coefficients in general -- remains open as of September 2026; the Wikipedia article on Kronecker coefficients still states this plainly and cites no resolution. Since the frozen revision date, two lines of genuine mathematical progress appeared. (1) Pak, Panova, Swanson, 'A combinatorial interpretation for certain plethysm and Kronecker coefficients' (arXiv:2511.02312, v1 posted 2025-11-04, revised through v3 on 2026-07-27), give an explicit positive rule -- counting certain marked trees -- for plethysm coefficients, which in the special case mu=(n) specializes to a combinatorial interpretation for the rectangular Kronecker coefficients g(lambda,(n^k),(n^k)) when lambda has at most two rows. This is a genuine restriction of the stated problem (a class of Kronecker coefficients, not a different question), so it counts as `partial` per the case/variant test in section 3.1: it removes real territory (all two-row-lambda rectangular cases) from the open problem, in the confirming direction (the object sought -- a positive combinatorial rule -- was shown to exist for this class). I read the full HTML/PDF text via WebFetch (introduction and available body text); no acknowledgements section or methods statement mentioning AI, machine learning, computer algebra search, or automated proof discovery appeared anywhere in the retrieved text, and the authors describe a traditional tree-theoretic proof technique. (2) Harman and Wilson, 'Kronecker Coefficients, Crystals, and Bitableaux' (arXiv:2507.14026, posted 2025-07-18), introduce 'bitableaux' as candidate combinatorial objects and reduce the general problem to a purified combinatorial conjecture, additionally proving a combinatorial expansion in the monomial-symmetric-function basis (weaker than a fully positive Schur-basis rule). This is progress/partial-flavored but is subsumed by the Pak-Panova-Swanson dating for the decisive event; I treat it as supporting context in `summary` rather than a second record, per the instruction to fold multiple events for one problem into the single decisive one. Separately, I found a cluster of machine-learning papers on Kronecker coefficients: Lee, 'Data-scientific study of Kronecker coefficients' (arXiv:2310.17906, 2023, predates the window) and Butbaia, Lee, Ruehle, 'Interpretable Machine Learning for Kronecker Coefficients' (arXiv:2502.11774, posted 2025-02-17), which train neural networks (including transformers, >99% accuracy) and interpretable models to predict whether a given Kronecker coefficient is zero or nonzero, and extract an ML-derived decision function in terms of 'b-loadings.' This is a different question from the stated problem: predicting vanishing is not a combinatorial rule for the value of g(lambda,mu,nu), and the paper itself does not claim to supply one -- it is a related/variant problem under section 3.1, not a case of this one, so it does not move the status and involves no claimed AI role in producing a result that is in scope here. No withdrawal, retraction, or dispute was found for any of these papers.
competing_reading: One could argue the ML vanishing-prediction papers (2310.17906, 2502.11774) are close enough to count as 'progress' with ai_role bound/assisted, since they do bear on Kronecker coefficients and use genuine AI systems (transformers). I judged them out of scope because the stated problem asks for a combinatorial interpretation (a rule explaining the value/multiplicity), whereas these papers only classify zero-vs-nonzero using black-box or semi-interpretable statistical models and do not produce, or claim to produce, a combinatorial formula -- so under section 3.1 they change a different bullet (nonvanishing/complexity questions), not this one. If a future reader takes a looser scope reading in which any AI-assisted numerical/structural insight about Kronecker coefficients counts, this record would need to add ai_role bound or assisted for those papers alongside a second, separate open question about vanishing.
what_would_settle_it: Whether the ML papers should be scoped into this bullet turns on the exact wording a careful reader would use for 'combinatorial interpretation' -- if that phrase is read broadly enough to include any explicit rule (even ML-derived heuristics) for a related invariant, the classification would need to change; a statement from the authors of the ML papers claiming their decision function constitutes a combinatorial interpretation (rather than a predictive classifier) would settle it in favor of inclusion.
